sciXsEngTest: A team tests a boat design in a calm pool, but the boat will be used on a windy lake. What is the weakness of this test?
The test conditions do not match real use
The pool water is too clean
Boats should never be tested in water
The test used too few materials
A good test should copy the conditions the design will actually face.
Three students test paper airplane designs, but each student throws a different plane. Why is this a problem?
Throwing strength is a variable that is not controlled
Paper airplanes cannot be measured
Three planes are too many to test
The planes should be thrown indoors only
If different people throw, differences in distance could come from the thrower instead of the design.
A phone case is dropped 10 times and cracks once. Another case is dropped once and does not crack. Which result is more reliable?
The case dropped 10 times, because it had more trials
The case dropped once, because it never cracked
Both are equally reliable no matter the trials
Neither, because drop tests are not useful
More trials give more reliable evidence about how a design performs.
The criterion for an insulated lunch box is to keep food cold for 4 hours. Which test best evaluates it?
Measure the food's temperature every hour for 4 hours
Weigh the lunch box when it is empty
Ask friends which colour they like best
Measure how long it takes to open the lid
The test should measure the property named in the criterion, which is keeping food cold over time.
A bridge model holds 2 kg in one trial, 2.1 kg in the next and 6 kg in the third. What should engineers do?
Check for an error and repeat the trials
Report only the 6 kg result
Average them and ignore the odd result
Stop testing because the design works
A result very different from the others may come from a mistake, so it should be checked and the test repeated.
Engineers test a new wind turbine blade on one very windy day only. What is a weakness of this test?
It does not show how the blade works in lighter winds
Wind turbines should be tested indoors only
One day is far too long for a test
Windy days make the blades heavier
Testing under only one condition does not show how the design performs across the conditions it will face.
Why do engineers record test results in a data table?
To organize results so designs can be compared
To make the test take longer
Because tables replace the need to test
To hide results that look wrong
A data table organizes measurements so patterns and comparisons are easy to see.
A team tests a backpack by asking only the designers if they like it. What is the problem with this test?
The designers may be biased toward their own design
Backpacks cannot be tested by people
The designers are not strong enough
Asking questions is always forbidden
People who made a design may favour it, so testing should include fair measurements or other users.
Two egg-drop designs are tested. One uses a large egg and one uses a small egg. Why is this a problem?
The egg size is a variable that should be the same
Eggs should never be used in tests
Small eggs always break first
Large eggs are too easy to drop
To compare designs fairly, everything except the design itself should be kept the same.
A water filter makes dirty water look clear. Why is this not enough evidence that the water is safe to drink?
Clear water can still contain germs or dissolved chemicals
Clear water is always unsafe
Filters cannot change how water looks
Water must be blue to be safe
Looking clear does not prove water is free of microbes or dissolved substances, so other tests are needed.
After testing, a chair design holds weight well but costs too much. What should engineers do next?
Redesign to lower the cost while keeping it strong
Give up on the whole project
Ignore the cost and build it anyway
Make it weaker to use more material
Test results show which criteria or constraints are not met so the design can be improved.
A team measures how far a toy car rolls, but they use a different ramp height for each car. What should they change?
Use the same ramp height for every car
Use a different car for every trial
Measure in centimetres for one car only
Paint all the cars the same colour
Keeping the ramp height constant makes the comparison fair.
What is a prototype?
An early model built to test a design
The final product sold in stores
A drawing of a different design
A list of materials to buy
A prototype is a working model used to test ideas before making the final version.
Why is it useful to test a design until it fails?
It shows the limits of the design
It proves the design is perfect
It saves all the materials
It makes the design stronger
Knowing where and when a design fails helps engineers understand its limits and improve it.
Two insulated cups are tested. One starts with water at 80 °C and the other at 60 °C. What is the problem?
The starting temperature should be the same
The cups should hold juice instead
80 °C is too cold for a test
Cups cannot be compared at all
A fair test starts both designs under the same conditions.
A test shows that a parachute design falls slowly but tangles often. Which conclusion is best?
It meets the speed criterion but needs work on reliability
It is a perfect design with no problems
It fails every criterion
Tangling does not matter in a parachute
Evaluating a test means checking each criterion separately, including both strengths and weaknesses.
A team tests a shoe sole for grip only on dry floors. What is missing?
A test of grip on wet or icy surfaces
A test of the shoe's colour
A test of the shoelace length
A test on a floor that is also dry
A shoe must grip on many surfaces, so testing only dry floors leaves out important conditions.
Why should test results be shared with other engineers?
Others can check the results and suggest improvements
So others can copy the design and sell it
Because sharing makes the results change
So the team does not need to test again
Sharing results allows others to review, repeat and improve on the work.
A sunscreen is tested on one person for 10 minutes. Why is this a weak test?
The sample is too small and the time is too short
Sunscreen does not need testing
Ten minutes is far too long
One person is too many people
Reliable tests use enough trials or subjects and run long enough to show real results.
Engineers test a model house in a wind tunnel at increasing speeds. What are they most likely measuring?
How much wind the house can withstand
How much the house costs to build
How warm the house stays in winter
How many rooms the house has
A wind tunnel test with increasing speeds checks how strong a structure is against wind.
A team tests a new cooler and finds ice melts in 6 hours. Their old cooler took 5 hours. What can they conclude?
The new cooler keeps ice longer than the old one
The new cooler is worse than the old one
Both coolers perform exactly the same
The test tells them nothing at all
Comparing to the old design shows the new cooler is an improvement, as ice lasts an hour longer.
What is the purpose of a control in testing a design?
To give a standard for comparing the results
To make the test cost more money
To change several variables at once
To guarantee the design will pass
A control or comparison shows whether the design actually makes a difference.
sciXsMoon: Why do astronauts on the Moon need spacesuits with their own air supply?
The Moon has almost no atmosphere to breathe
The Moon's air is too hot to breathe
Moon air is full of smoke
Astronauts must hold their breath on the Moon
With almost no atmosphere, the Moon has no breathable air, so suits must supply oxygen.
Moon dust is very sharp and sticky. Which design feature would help most?
Seals that keep dust out of joints and equipment
Bright paint on the outside of the rover
Larger windows in the lander
Softer seats inside the cabin
Sharp lunar dust can damage moving parts, so seals protect equipment.
Why are rockets built in stages that drop away?
Dropping empty stages makes the rocket lighter
Stages make the rocket look taller
Dropping stages slows the rocket down
Each stage carries a separate astronaut
Getting rid of empty fuel tanks reduces mass, so the remaining fuel can push the rocket faster.
A Moon base must be built using as few materials from Earth as possible. Why?
Launching mass from Earth is very expensive
Earth materials melt on the Moon
Moon rules ban Earth materials
Earth materials are too light to use
Every kilogram launched costs a lot of fuel and money, which is a major constraint.
Gravity on the Moon is about 1/6 of Earth's. How does this affect a rover design?
Its wheels must still grip on low gravity and loose dust
It needs no wheels at all
It must be much heavier to stay down
It can only move at night
Low gravity means less weight pressing the wheels down, so engineers design wheels for grip on dust.
Why might a Moon base be built near the lunar south pole?
Ice may be found in shadowy craters there
It is the warmest place on the Moon
It is the only place with air
It is closest to the Sun
Scientists think ice exists in permanently shadowed craters near the poles, which could supply water.
Which is a criterion for a Moon rover?
It must travel across rough, rocky ground
It must be cheaper than a bicycle
It must float in lunar oceans
It must work without any power
A criterion describes what the design must do to succeed, such as crossing rough terrain.
Why do engineers use computer simulations before building a lunar lander?
To test ideas safely and cheaply before building
Because simulations replace all real testing
To make the lander heavier
Because the Moon cannot be studied
Simulations let engineers test many ideas without the cost and risk of building each one.
Engineers have two lander designs. Design A is lighter; Design B is stronger. What should they do?
Compare both designs against the criteria and constraints
Always pick the one with a cooler name
Pick whichever was drawn first
Build neither and start over
Choosing among solutions means weighing how well each meets the criteria and constraints.
Why do Moon habitats need thick walls or covering soil?
To block radiation and tiny meteorites
To keep the Moon's wind out
To hold in the Moon's oxygen
To make the habitat float
Without an atmosphere, the Moon's surface is exposed to radiation and micrometeorites.
Why do solar panels work well for power on most of the Moon's surface?
Sunlight is not blocked by clouds or air
The Moon makes its own sunlight
The Moon is always in daylight
Solar panels need no sunlight on the Moon
With no atmosphere, sunlight reaches the surface directly, though long lunar nights still need stored power.
A night on the Moon lasts about two Earth weeks. What design problem does this create?
Equipment needs stored power and heat to survive
Astronauts cannot sleep for two weeks
Rovers must drive twice as fast
Solar panels make too much power
During the long, cold lunar night there is no sunlight, so batteries and heaters are needed.
Why do engineers brainstorm many ideas before choosing one?
Considering many ideas makes a better solution more likely
It is required to use all the ideas
Brainstorming replaces testing
The first idea is always the worst
Generating several possible solutions helps engineers find the one that best fits the criteria.
A spacecraft must fit inside the nose cone of a rocket. This is an example of a…
size constraint
test result
scientific law
prototype
The nose cone sets a limit on the spacecraft's size, so it is a constraint.
Why would engineers reuse water on a Moon base?
Water is heavy to bring from Earth and scarce on the Moon
Water on the Moon is too salty
Reusing water makes it heavier
Astronauts do not need water
Recycling water reduces how much must be launched from Earth.
How do Moon landers slow down before touching down?
They fire rocket engines downward
They open large parachutes
They glide on wings through the air
They bounce off the clouds
With no air for parachutes or wings, landers use rocket engines to slow their fall.
Why are lunar spacesuits tested in vacuum chambers on Earth?
A vacuum chamber copies the airless conditions on the Moon
Vacuum chambers make suits lighter
Vacuum chambers add Moon gravity
Spacesuits are cleaned in vacuum chambers
Testing in a vacuum lets engineers check that suits work in conditions like the Moon's.
A rover keeps getting stuck in sand during a test. What is the best next step?
Change the wheel design and test again
Launch the rover to the Moon anyway
Stop testing because it failed once
Paint the rover a lighter colour
Engineers use test failures to improve the design and then retest it.
Why do engineers communicate with the public and other teams about a Moon mission?
To share results, gain feedback and support
To keep the mission a total secret
Because talking replaces engineering
To change the laws of physics
Sharing designs and results helps teams improve ideas and keeps the public informed.
Why can radio messages from the Moon reach Earth, but sound cannot?
Radio waves travel through space, but sound needs matter
Sound is too slow to leave the Moon
Radio waves need air to travel
The Moon blocks all sound waves
Sound needs a medium such as air, but radio waves can travel through the vacuum of space.
Which is a trade-off in designing a Moon rover?
Adding more batteries gives more range but adds mass
Bigger wheels always make it lighter
Adding cameras removes the need for power
Painting it white makes it faster
A trade-off means improving one feature makes another worse, like range versus mass.
Why do Moon missions often send robots before people?
Robots can explore safely and gather data first
Robots are always cheaper than paper
People are not allowed to visit the Moon
Robots can breathe Moon air
Robotic missions reduce risk by scouting conditions before humans arrive.
sciXsAbForce: What is the symbol for watt (power)?
The watt, the unit of power, uses the symbol W.
What is the symbol for coulomb (electric charge)?
The coulomb, the unit of charge, uses the symbol C.
What is the symbol for kilojoule?
The prefix kilo is a lowercase k, and joule is a capital J.
What is the symbol for kilowatt?
Kilo uses a lowercase k and watt uses a capital W.
What is the symbol for milliampere?
Milli uses a lowercase m and ampere uses a capital A.
What is the symbol for kilonewton?
Kilo uses a lowercase k and newton uses a capital N.
What is the symbol for kilovolt?
Kilo uses a lowercase k and volt uses a capital V.
What is the symbol for megawatt?
Mega uses a capital M, and watt uses a capital W; mW would mean milliwatt.
What is the symbol for millivolt?
Milli uses a lowercase m; MV would mean megavolt.
What is the symbol for kilowatt-hour (electrical energy)?
A kilowatt-hour is written kWh: lowercase k, capital W, lowercase h.
What is the symbol for megajoule?
Mega uses a capital M and joule uses a capital J.
What is the symbol for kilohm?
Kilo uses a lowercase k and ohm uses the Greek letter omega, Ω.
Which unit does the symbol N stand for?
N is the symbol for the newton, the SI unit of force.
Which unit does the symbol J stand for?
J is the symbol for the joule, the SI unit of energy.
Which unit does the symbol W stand for?
W is the symbol for the watt, the SI unit of power.
Which unit does the symbol V stand for?
V is the symbol for the volt, the SI unit of electric potential difference.
Which unit does the symbol A stand for?
A is the symbol for the ampere, the SI unit of electric current.
Which unit does the symbol Ω stand for?
Ω is the symbol for the ohm, the SI unit of electrical resistance.
Which unit does the symbol C stand for?
In electricity, C is the symbol for the coulomb, the unit of charge.
Which is the correct way to write 5 kilowatts?
The kilo prefix is a lowercase k, and units named after people use a capital letter.
Which is the correct way to write 250 milliamperes?
Milli is a lowercase m and ampere is a capital A.
Which is the correct way to write 12 newtons?
The newton's symbol is a single capital N.
sciDensCmp: Gold has a density of 19.3 g/cm³ and aluminum has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. Which is denser?
Gold has the greater mass per cubic centimetre, so it is denser.
A wooden block (0.6 g/cm³) is placed in water (1.0 g/cm³). What happens?
An object less dense than water floats.
Two balls are the same size. Ball X has a mass of 50 g and Ball Y has a mass of 20 g. Which is denser?
With equal volumes, the one with more mass is denser.
Two objects have the same mass. Object P has a volume of 10 cm³ and Object Q has a volume of 40 cm³. Which is denser?
The same mass packed into a smaller volume means greater density.
Honey (1.4 g/cm³), water (1.0 g/cm³) and vegetable oil (0.9 g/cm³) are poured into a jar. Which layer ends up on the bottom?
The densest liquid sinks to the bottom.
Honey (1.4 g/cm³), water (1.0 g/cm³) and vegetable oil (0.9 g/cm³) are poured into a jar. Which layer ends up on top?
The least dense liquid floats on top.
A plastic toy sinks in water but floats in salt water. What does this tell you?
Salt water is denser than fresh water
Fresh water is denser than salt water
The toy got lighter in salt water
Salt water and fresh water are equally dense
An object floats in a liquid denser than itself, so salt water must be denser than fresh water.
A steel nail sinks in water, but a large steel ship floats. Why?
The ship's hollow shape gives it a lower overall density
The ship is made of lighter steel
The ship has less mass than the nail
The ship encloses lots of air, so its average density is less than water.
Which is denser: 1 kg of feathers or 1 kg of iron?
They have the same mass, but iron takes up much less volume, so it is denser.
A piece of clay is rolled into a long snake shape. What happens to its density?
Changing the shape does not change the mass or volume, so density stays the same.
Mercury has a density of 13.6 g/cm³. Would a steel bolt (7.8 g/cm³) sink or float in mercury?
Steel is less dense than mercury, so it floats on mercury.
Granite is 2.7 g/cm³ and pumice is 0.6 g/cm³. Which rock could float on water?
Pumice is less dense than water (1.0 g/cm³), so it can float; granite sinks.
A grape sinks in water. What can you say about its density?
It is the same as air
Objects that sink in water are denser than water's 1.0 g/cm³.
Hot air rises above cool air. Which is less dense?
Heated air expands, so its density decreases and it rises.
Substance A: 30 g in 10 cm³. Substance B: 30 g in 15 cm³. Which is denser?
A has a density of 3 g/cm³ and B has 2 g/cm³, so A is denser.
Substance A: 12 g in 4 cm³. Substance B: 20 g in 10 cm³. Which is denser?
A is 3 g/cm³ and B is 2 g/cm³, so A is denser even though B has more mass.
A small pebble sinks in water, but a large log floats. Which statement is correct?
The pebble is denser than the log
The log is denser than the pebble
The pebble has more mass than the log
Sinking or floating depends on density, not size, so the pebble is denser.
A block of ice (0.92 g/cm³) is placed in vegetable oil (0.9 g/cm³). What happens?
Ice is slightly denser than vegetable oil, so it sinks in oil.
A cube of copper is cut into four smaller pieces. How does the density of each piece compare to the original?
It is one quarter as much
Density is a property of the substance, so it does not change when the sample is cut.
Which material is the least dense? Lead 11.3 g/cm³, aluminum 2.7 g/cm³, iron 7.9 g/cm³, cork 0.24 g/cm³
Cork has the smallest density of the four.
Which material is the most dense? Silver 10.5 g/cm³, glass 2.5 g/cm³, ice 0.92 g/cm³, oak wood 0.75 g/cm³
Silver has the largest density of the four materials.
Why does a helium balloon rise in the air?
Helium is less dense than air
Helium has no mass at all
A gas less dense than the surrounding air rises.
sciAccel: Which object is accelerating?
A skateboarder speeding up down a hill
A book resting on a desk
A car moving at a steady 50 km/h in a straight line
A ship sailing straight at a constant speed
Speeding up is a change in velocity, so the skateboarder is accelerating.
Which object is NOT accelerating?
An elevator rising at a constant speed
A car turning a corner
A ball slowing as it rolls on grass
A sled speeding up down a hill
Constant speed in a straight line means the velocity is not changing.
Which object is accelerating?
A Ferris wheel seat moving in a circle at constant speed
A lamp sitting on a table
A plane flying straight at constant speed
A train stopped at a station
Moving in a circle changes direction constantly, so the seat is accelerating.
Which object is NOT accelerating?
A hockey puck gliding straight at a steady speed on smooth ice
A puck that is slowed by a stick
A puck hit so it speeds up
A puck that bounces off the boards
A puck moving at a constant speed in a straight line has constant velocity.
A cyclist brakes and slows down. Is the cyclist accelerating?
Yes, because the speed is changing
No, because the cyclist is slowing down
No, because the direction is the same
Yes, because the cyclist is moving
Any change in speed, including slowing down, is acceleration.
A car drives around a roundabout at a steady 30 km/h. Is it accelerating?
Yes, because its direction is changing
No, because its speed is constant
No, because 30 km/h is slow
Yes, because its speed is increasing
Acceleration is a change in velocity, and velocity includes direction.
A rock rests on the ground. Is it accelerating?
No, because its velocity is not changing
Yes, because gravity pulls on it
Yes, because Earth is under it
No, because rocks have no mass
An object at rest with balanced forces has a constant velocity of zero.
A soccer ball is kicked and leaves the ground. At the moment of the kick, is the ball accelerating?
Yes, because its speed increases quickly
No, because the foot stops touching it
No, because it was not moving before
Yes, because it is on the ground
The kick changes the ball's speed from zero, which is acceleration.
A rocket lifts off and goes faster and faster. Is it accelerating?
Yes, because its speed is increasing
No, because it moves straight up
No, because rockets move at constant speed
Yes, because it is very heavy
Increasing speed means the rocket's velocity is changing.
A ball is thrown straight up and slows as it rises. Is it accelerating?
Yes, because its speed is decreasing
No, because it is going up
No, because it has not stopped yet
Yes, because it is getting heavier
Gravity slows the ball, changing its velocity, so it accelerates.
A truck travels on a straight highway at a steady 100 km/h. Is it accelerating?
No, because its speed and direction are constant
Yes, because 100 km/h is fast
Yes, because the engine is running
No, because trucks cannot accelerate
Constant speed in a straight line means zero acceleration.
Which object is accelerating?
A swing slowing down as it reaches the top
A parked car on a flat street
A box sitting on a shelf
A cruise ship sailing straight at steady speed
The swing's speed is changing, so it is accelerating.
Which object is NOT accelerating?
A drone hovering in one place
A drone speeding up as it climbs
A drone turning in a circle
A drone slowing to land
A hovering drone stays still, so its velocity does not change.
A child on a merry-go-round moves at a steady speed. Why is the child accelerating?
The child's direction keeps changing
The child's speed keeps increasing
The child is not moving at all
The child's mass keeps changing
Circular motion means a constant change in direction, which is acceleration.
A runner keeps a steady pace along a straight track. What is the runner's acceleration?
It is zero
It is increasing
It equals the speed
It is decreasing
With no change in speed or direction, the acceleration is zero.
A car's speedometer reads 60 km/h, then 70 km/h, then 80 km/h on a straight road. What is the car doing?
Accelerating by speeding up
Moving at constant velocity
Accelerating by turning
Decelerating as it slows
The speed is increasing, so the car is accelerating.
A car's speedometer stays at 60 km/h as it follows a curved road. What is the car doing?
Accelerating by changing direction
Moving at constant velocity
Accelerating by speeding up
Standing still on the road
Following a curve changes direction, so the car accelerates even at constant speed.
Which change does NOT count as acceleration?
Moving the same speed in the same direction
Speeding up
Slowing down
Changing direction
Acceleration is any change in speed or direction, so no change means no acceleration.
A skydiver falls at a steady terminal speed. Is the skydiver accelerating?
No, because the speed and direction are constant
Yes, because the skydiver is falling
Yes, because gravity always accelerates
No, because the skydiver is not moving
At terminal speed, air resistance balances gravity, so velocity stays constant.
A hockey player skates around the net in a curve without changing speed. Is the player accelerating?
Yes, because the direction is changing
No, because the speed stays the same
No, because ice has no friction
Yes, because the speed is increasing
A change in direction is a change in velocity, so it is acceleration.
A subway train pulls into a station and comes to a stop. Is it accelerating while it stops?
Yes, because its speed is decreasing
No, because it is stopping
No, because it travels underground
Yes, because its direction is reversing
Slowing down is a change in velocity, so the train accelerates.
The Moon orbits Earth. Is the Moon accelerating?
Yes, because its direction keeps changing
No, because it is far from Earth
No, because space has no air
Yes, because it is speeding up forever
Moving in a curved orbit means the Moon's direction, and so its velocity, is always changing.
sciNewton: A person steps off a small boat onto a dock. What happens to the boat?
The boat moves away from the dock
The boat moves toward the dock
The boat stays perfectly still
The boat sinks straight down
The person pushes the boat backward as they push themselves forward, so the boat moves the other way.
A cannon fires a cannonball forward. What happens to the cannon?
It recoils backward
It moves forward with the ball
It stays completely still
It lifts straight upward
The cannon pushes the ball forward, and the ball pushes the cannon backward with an equal force.
You push on a box with 30 N. How hard does the box push on you?
30 N, in the opposite direction
30 N, in the same direction
15 N, in the opposite direction
0 N, because boxes cannot push
Newton's third law says forces come in equal and opposite pairs.
A balloon is let go and air rushes out of the back. Which way does the balloon move?
Forward, away from the escaping air
Backward, with the escaping air
Straight down to the floor
It does not move at all
The balloon pushes air out the back, and the air pushes the balloon the opposite way.
A person walks forward. Which way do their feet push on the ground?
Backward
Forward
Upward only
They do not push
Your feet push the ground backward, and the ground pushes you forward.
A book rests on a table. The book pushes down on the table. What does the table do?
Pushes up on the book with an equal force
Pushes down on the book
Pulls the book sideways
Does nothing to the book
The table exerts an equal and opposite upward force on the book.
A canoeist pushes the paddle backward through the water. What does the water do?
Pushes the canoe forward
Pushes the canoe backward
Pulls the canoe down
Stops the canoe from moving
The water pushes forward on the paddle, moving the canoe forward.
A small car and a large truck collide. Which feels the larger force?
Both feel forces of the same size
The small car feels a larger force
The large truck feels a larger force
Neither vehicle feels any force
By Newton's third law, the forces are equal and opposite, though the car accelerates more.
Two skaters stand face to face and push off each other. What happens?
They both move apart in opposite directions
Only the stronger skater moves
They both move in the same direction
Neither skater moves at all
Each skater pushes the other, so both receive a force in opposite directions.
A jet engine pushes hot gas backward. What does the gas do to the plane?
Pushes the plane forward
Pushes the plane backward
Pulls the plane down
Has no effect on the plane
The gas pushes back on the engine with an equal and opposite force, moving the plane forward.
A fish pushes water backward with its tail. What does the water do?
Pushes the fish forward
Pushes the fish backward
Pulls the fish to the bottom
Nothing at all
The water pushes the fish forward with an equal and opposite force.
A soccer player kicks a ball. What does the ball do to the player's foot?
Pushes back on the foot with equal force
Pulls the foot forward
Pushes the foot with a smaller force
Exerts no force on the foot
The ball exerts a force on the foot equal in size and opposite in direction.
A rifle is fired. Why does it push back against the shooter's shoulder?
The bullet pushes back on the rifle as the rifle pushes it forward
The rifle gets heavier when fired
Air pulls the rifle backward
The shoulder pushes the rifle forward
The forces on the bullet and the rifle are an equal and opposite pair.
A swimmer pushes off the wall of a pool. What pushes the swimmer forward?
The wall pushing on the swimmer
The swimmer pushing on the wall
The water pulling the swimmer
Gravity pulling the swimmer
The swimmer pushes the wall, and the wall pushes the swimmer forward.
A garden hose sprays water forward. What happens to the nozzle?
It is pushed backward
It is pushed forward
It is pulled downward
It feels no force
The water is pushed out forward, so the water pushes the nozzle backward.
Earth pulls the Moon toward it with gravity. What does the Moon do to Earth?
Pulls Earth toward the Moon with an equal force
Pushes Earth away from it
Pulls Earth with a much smaller force
Exerts no force on Earth
Gravitational forces also come in equal and opposite pairs.
A person on roller skates throws a heavy ball forward. What happens to the person?
They roll backward
They roll forward
They stay still
They spin in a circle
The person pushes the ball forward, and the ball pushes the person backward.
A hockey stick hits a puck with a force of 40 N. What force does the puck exert on the stick?
40 N, in the opposite direction
40 N, in the same direction
20 N, in the opposite direction
80 N, in the opposite direction
The puck pushes back on the stick with an equal and opposite force.
A squid shoots water out of its body backward. What happens to the squid?
It moves forward
It moves backward
It sinks
It stops moving
Pushing water backward makes the water push the squid forward.
A helicopter's blades push air downward. What does the air do?
Pushes the helicopter upward
Pushes the helicopter downward
Pulls the helicopter sideways
Does nothing to the helicopter
The air pushes back up on the blades, lifting the helicopter.
You lean against a tree and push on it. Why don't you fall into the tree?
The tree pushes back on you with an equal force
The tree pulls you toward it
You stop pushing as you lean
Gravity stops working on you
The tree exerts an equal and opposite force that supports you.
A bowling ball hits a pin. Compared with the force the ball exerts on the pin, the force the pin exerts on the ball is…
equal and opposite
larger and opposite
smaller and in the same direction
zero

What is the common name of Branta canadensis?
